anti_generic_signature_read: Ranked cold, unprompted: "1. The pieces are the eight planets and are sized relative to each other. This is the strongest idea in the object. A set where your king-equivalent is Jupiter because Jupiter is physically the biggest thing you own is a genuinely good piece of design reasoning -- the hierarchy is legible without a rulebook. 2. The Earth piece is actually mapped. It is the only piece with real cartography rather than a decorative band or spot. You can turn it in your fingers and find an Atlantic and a Pacific. That's a reason to pick that one piece up and look at it, which is more than most game pieces earn. 3. The board has terrain rather than uniform squares, with two colour-keyed opposing zones and a debris barrier between them. 4. The disc-plus-sphere piece form, and its matching eight-recess tray." The correction's own promise came second on that list, written by a reader who had not been told a correction existed.
blind_action_read: "Moment to moment I think a person picks up one planet by its sphere -- the sphere is a handle, the wide disc is the thing that lands -- and sets it down on a square... Because the pieces are all different sizes and all instantly distinguishable at a glance across the table, I'd expect play to involve recognising 'that's their Jupiter' from three feet away, which is exactly what the size ladder buys you... the two sunburst-and-spike zones at opposite corners are places you are trying to reach or defend. Between turns, captured pieces go nose-down into the eight recesses in your tray."
blind_form_read: "One dominant flat slab: a rectangular grey board scored into a square grid, the base mass everything else reads against. Sixteen small vertical masses stand on it, each a low cylindrical puck about 1.7 times the diameter of the ball it carries, with a sphere seated on top through a short collar; these are the only things that stand to grabbable height. Two terrain families are set into the grid rather than standing on it: ochre rubble cells with a raised crumbly rim around a smooth circular floor, and two four-cell star clusters whose centre plates are flat, one pale cream and slightly proud, one pure black. About fourteen slender tapered cones are the only sharp vertical features. Two thin off-board trays lie beside the board, each with eight wells." And: "the spheres are deliberately sized differently from each other... that size ladder is one of the more deliberate things in the design."
blind_held_read: "A two-player abstract strategy board game about the solar system. If I picked it up I would say I was holding a printed game board tile-set: a flat grey slab scored into a square grid, sixteen ball-on-disc playing pieces (two colour-coded armies of eight), a set of drop-in terrain tiles, and two off-board storage trays with nests. It reads as 'chess, but the pieces are planets and the two home squares are a sun and an anti-sun'."
blind_relationship_read: "The grammar is: board contains squares; squares receive bases; bases carry spheres; trays receive bases. The disc is the grammatical joint of the whole thing -- it is what talks to the square and what talks to the tray recess, and it is the reason every piece has the same footprint despite the spheres varying hugely in size... Spatially the two terrain zones sit at diagonally opposite corners and the debris field runs as a diagonal barrier between them, so the board has an implied axis of travel... Identity lives in the sphere, function lives in the base."
blind_subjects_read: All eight planets named cold, from surface alone: Jupiter from "horizontal orange/tan bands and a single red oval spot... the Great Red Spot and nothing else looks like that"; Saturn from "a flat protruding ring"; Uranus and Neptune as a pale-cyan/deep-blue banded pair; Mars as "a small, uniformly bright red sphere"; Mercury and Venus as the two plain ones; and "A small blue-and-green sphere with white patches. Earth, very high confidence." Then the board: "an asteroid belt or debris field"; both star clusters, "The two zones are diagonally opposite"; "Two separate flat trays, each with eight shallow circular recesses"; and the numerals, "On the two Earth pieces the mark reads as a pixelated '4'."

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Named cold, before any brief: "A small blue-and-green sphere with white patches. Earth, very high confidence." Per face: "Yes -- Earth, Atlantic-facing"; "Yes -- Earth, Atlantic-facing, and I am more confident here than in image 3"; "Yes -- the Pacific hemisphere of Earth." The shapes did the work: South America "broad at the top and comes to a point at the bottom", Africa "the right-limb green with a grey lozenge across it reads as Africa with the Sahara", Australia "that isolated island with a desert-coloured interior ringed by green coast". The words this correction existed to remove -- blob, mottled, marble -- appear nowhere in the blind text.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. Both Earth globes must read as the real Earth: recognisable continent coastlines, not circles. A person who picks up the Sol world should be able to name what they are looking at without being told.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Three of the four were named blind: "The lower-left tapering mass is a convincing South America... The green top-left is North America"; "a convincing Africa-with-Sahara plus Arabia"; "which reads as Australia". Eurasia did not resolve blind -- "an abstract green stripe" -- because neither required frame presents it: on one it is over the limb, on the other the foreshortened northern rim. Round two added snap/worlds/earth-*-eurasia.png at azimuth 70, disclosed to the critic as non-blind, and it resolved on structure: "two separate green masses joined only around a narrow neck, with a blue wedge biting in between them", the lower carrying the Sahara and the upper inner Asia -- "Two continents, separated by a Mediterranean-shaped sea, joined at a Suez-shaped neck, each with its own correctly placed desert. That is Eurasia." Stated plainly: three groups blind, the fourth on a frame seen after the Wish was revealed.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. The green land is built from the coastlines of the Americas, Africa, Eurasia and Australia.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: "a long grey lozenge lying on top of it" -- on top of the green, so interior; and the cleanest case, Australia: "a closed green ring... with a grey-taupe core inside it", a desert wholly enclosed by its own coast. Inner Asia and the American southwest were read as patches "sitting within the green band".
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. The beige dryland is subtracted out of the land, so it sits inside a continent rather than beside it.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Twice, before the critic knew this was a requirement: "lobed, with a notch bitten out of its lower edge" and "a large white blob... with a downward finger". The cap was never described as a circle or a lid. Round two added the one view that could falsify it, straight down each piece's own pole: "the white mass's boundary has at least six concave/convex reversals... and nowhere does it follow a circle. If this were a lid laid on the sphere, a plan view is precisely where it would show as a disc, and it does not."
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. The white ice must not read as a lid laid on the globe: the northern cap's rim is broken by lobes instead of ending on an exact circle of latitude.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Four distinct surface colours were read on every face without prompting: "blue ocean", "bright green land", "pure white patches", and a fourth pale one the critic called "light grey" and "grey-taupe". The four regions are there and separate. That the fourth reads as grey rather than sand is beige #F7E6DE doing what a very pale warm white does at this size; it is the filament the set already used and the correction was required to keep it. Recorded as a legibility limitation, not a missing region.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. Earth keeps its blue globe, green land, beige dryland and white ice -- four filaments, four regions.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: The fatal error would have been a reflected Earth on one army, and the critic tested for it unprompted: "They are not mirror images -- I checked chirality specifically, by which side the tapering mass and the grey desert sit on, and both images put the taper on the left and the desert on the right. Handedness is consistent." Round two made it rigorous with a five-landmark cyclic-order test across the two polar frames: "A reflection cannot be produced by a rotation. The map is not mirrored." The inversions read under one camera: "the Sol globe's white sits up-and-left of its centre while the Anti globe's pale streak sits up-and-right", and "black glyph on ivory, grey glyph on black, identical block pattern". The Anti-Sol taper the black filament hid is measured instead: the Sol disc's widest circle is its filleted top at 33.874 mm, the Anti-Sol disc's its bed face at 34.000 mm.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. The Sol world leans its north pole toward +X and the Anti-Sol world toward -X, and the two remain mirrors of one another -- lean, disc taper and disc colour all inverted, while the map itself is identical on both and is NOT mirrored.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Inventoried cold: "eight distinct sculpts, each existing in a white-based and a black-based copy -- sixteen total, which matches the two eight-recess trays exactly"; the belt as "an asteroid belt or debris field"; both star clusters, "The two zones are diagonally opposite"; "Two separate flat trays, each with eight shallow circular recesses". The collar was read as part of the piece, never as a joint.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: POSITIVE. The rest of the set is unchanged and complete: eight planets in a visible size ladder, two armies of eight, the four-panel terrain board, twelve belt tiles, two opposed stars with six corona cells, two eight-well trays, no assembly and no hardware.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Asked point-blank, blind: "Does anything protrude from or stand proud of any sphere's surface? In the four close-ups, no. The continents, ice and deserts are flush colour regions coplanar with the sphere -- there is no embossing, no relief, no geometry standing above the surface anywhere on the Earth pieces." Round two, on the five new frames: "every globe silhouette is a clean arc with no bump, lip or step anywhere a marking meets the limb, and no patch shows a side-wall band of a different shade at its boundary." A buried wall cannot be seen from outside at all, and the critic said so; the proof is that part_world_earth_sol.step and part_world_earth_anti.step are byte-identical to the published ones, so no surface of the printed solid moved in any direction, and both passed the 45-degree overhang gate in this run.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. Nothing protrudes. The globe's outer surface stays a true sphere, no wall of an outline tool is ever exposed, and nothing a marking adds can face downward -- so the overhang-driven wall lean the source atlas was drawn for is not present.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: The blind vocabulary is coastline vocabulary, not blob vocabulary: "broad at the top and comes to a point at the bottom", "a long grey lozenge", "lobed, with a notch bitten out of its lower edge". A union of circles does not produce "broad at the top and comes to a point at the bottom". The critic did flag three small patches blind as hexagons, and withdrew two of the three in round two on seeing them away from the limb: "They were elongated shapes foreshortened at the limb, and I called them wrong." Australia it declined to clear, because no supplied frame shows it near the centre of the disc; that is carried openly as the largest remaining risk.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. Earth's markings must not read as circles or blobs.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: "the other seven read blind exactly as blob-based worlds should -- 'a red ball, a grey ball, a banded ball' -- with no sign of coastline-style outlines leaking onto them", and the critic said plainly that an image cannot prove a negative about a before-state. It is proved deterministically instead: twenty of the twenty-four printed geometries are byte-identical to the published set and the other four differ by one non-geometric STEP instance label, checked line by line (measure/revision-part-hashes.md); and occurrence by occurrence, 136 of the set's colour bodies match the published assembly on solid count, exact volume and bounding box, with every difference belonging to earth_sol_* or earth_anti_* (measure/occurrence-geometry.md).
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. Nothing but the two Earth pieces changed.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: The critic listed what it missed, unprompted: "no Panama isthmus", "no Philippines or Indonesia", "no Japan", "no New Zealand". Three of those were already disclosed; Japan and New Zealand were not, and the disclosure list was extended with a reason for each before round two rather than the geometry being changed. The critic's verdict on that: "Japan at about 0.3 mm wide cannot carry a colour boundary on both sides through a 0.4 mm nozzle -- you would get a merged smear or a gap, either of which is worse than absence. Dropping it is the correct call, not a shortcut... What was a defect at round 1 was the evidence package, not the part." Every omission now carries its reason in measure/earth-atlas-resolution.md.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE. No landmass was silently dropped.

largest_risk: Australia. It is the one marking the correction did not lift out of the old vocabulary, and the critic would not clear it in any of three rounds: blind it read as "a closed green ring... with a grey-taupe core inside it" and "a smooth rounded blob with none of Australia's actual outline", and having withdrawn its two other blob complaints as its own limb-foreshortening error it held this one open -- "it remains the weakest marking in the set and the one place the old blob vocabulary still fits". The cause is in the supplied atlas rather than in this build: Australia's eleven-vertex ring is 14.8 mm of perimeter on a 16.70 mm globe, and the outback fills so much of its interior that what is left is a green rim about two millimetres wide. Every other landmass reads; Australia reads as an island with a desert, which is true but is not its silhouette. Second, and unresolvable inside this correction's scope: beige #F7E6DE against white on a 16.70 mm globe. The critic called the dryland grey in every single blind description and in one place could not tell it from ice. Both filaments were required to stay. Third, a property of the repair rather than of the artifact, written down because a later reader will otherwise call it a fault: the two Earth colour bodies are no longer bit-reproducible between builds. The retry loop searches until two checkers accept, and this kernel does not return the same boolean answer twice, so rebuild-and-diff is not a valid integrity check for those two parts. All twenty-four printed solids remain reproducible; section 11.15 of antisol_spec.md records the measured numbers.
resolution: Three rounds; the third returns no blocking defect and no regression. A reader told nothing named the piece as Earth with very high confidence, named South America, North America, Africa and Australia from their outlines, and read the Sahara as a desert inside a continent and the ice as lobed rather than a lid. The word blob is absent from the blind text. Round one's four open items closed on evidence. Eurasia did not resolve because neither required frame presents it: three frames at azimuth 70 were added and it resolved as two continents across a Mediterranean. Two frames down each piece's own leaning pole show the cap is no lid. measure/earth-ice-cap.md samples 0.10 mm under the sphere and finds ice or land at every longitude above 72 degrees, so the cap is closed and the dark slot near the date line is the atlas's own water between ice lobes 4 and 5. Japan and New Zealand were missing from the disclosure list, so it gained a measured reason for each. Then the gate refused one body, earth_sol_land3_green, invalidTopology. Both repairs sit in the acceptance test, not the design: the clip loop now asks the topology checker too, and its retry gained a second axis turning the marking frame up to 0.23 degrees, 0.03 mm of arc. No dimension, ring, filament, ordering or subtraction changed; all 24 printed solids rebuilt byte-identical; inspect validate reports 178 occurrences, 0 failures, and the pipeline passes. Measurement settled the rest. Both Earth globes are 16.700 mm. The Sol disc's widest circle is its filleted top at 33.874 mm and the Anti-Sol disc's its bed face at 34.000 mm -- the taper inversion black filament hides. The two Earth printed solids are byte-identical to the published ones, so nothing here added a protrusion or a down-facing wall, and 136 occurrences match the published assembly exactly. Print readiness is not claimed: every part passed wall and overhang at 0.4 mm and 45 degrees, but nothing has been printed. Motion is unverified, never passed.
reviewer: One independent native critic, three rounds: six images and no brief, sealed; then the Wish revealed and each requirement checked against those answers; then every image regenerated and re-read.
